children.name: Sepsis Prediction
children.blurb: Sepsis prediction uses machine learning on electronic health record data to estimate a patient's risk of developing sepsis, often hours before clinical deterioration is obvious.

children.name: Acute Kidney Injury Prediction
children.blurb: Acute kidney injury prediction in intensive care uses routinely collected patient data to estimate the likelihood that a patient will develop AKI within a defined window, often 24 to 72 hours.

children.name: Ventilator Weaning
children.blurb: Ventilator weaning models estimate when a patient on mechanical ventilation is ready to breathe without the machine, or predict the chance that an extubation attempt will fail.

children.name: Fall Risk Monitoring
children.blurb: Fall risk monitoring in predictive patient analytics and intensive care uses clinical data to estimate a patient's chance of falling during a hospital stay or after discharge.

children.name: Staffing and Bed Forecasting
children.blurb: Staffing and bed forecasting uses predictive models to estimate patient admissions, discharges, transfers, and acuity in hospitals, especially intensive care units.

sections.body: This section covers predictive patient analytics in intensive care, where machine learning models process vital signs, lab results, and electronic health record data to estimate risks before they become obvious. In current practice, sepsis prediction tools flag patients whose heart rate, temperature, and white cell count patterns match earlier cases, while acute kidney injury models watch creatinine and urine output trends. Ventilator weaning systems suggest when a patient may tolerate a spontaneous breathing trial, and fall risk monitors use bed sensors and mobility scores to alert staff. Staffing and bed forecasting models predict admission volumes and lengths of stay so units can adjust nurse ratios and open beds. These are operational tools, not autonomous decision makers, and they run alongside clinical judgment.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Sepsis prediction has many published models and some hospital deployments, but performance drops when a model trained in one hospital is used in another, and false alarms remain common. Acute kidney injury prediction is more reliable for short horizons, often 24 to 48 hours, but less useful for longer term kidney decline. Ventilator weaning support is still largely assistive, with no model able to replace a clinician's assessment of readiness. Fall risk monitoring works best in controlled ward settings and poorly when patients move unexpectedly or sensors fail. Staffing and bed forecasting is the most operationally mature, but it depends on clean admission data and cannot predict sudden mass casualty events. Across the 1000 medical AI models tracked on this site, only a small share have been validated in multiple intensive care units, and the six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies show that real harm can occur when predictions are trusted too far.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for early warning systems should start with Sepsis Prediction, which explains the most studied use case and its alert fatigue problem. Acute Kidney Injury Prediction follows naturally because kidney stress often appears alongside sepsis, and the two pages share data sources like creatinine and urine output. Ventilator Weaning moves from detection to intervention, showing how predictions feed decisions about removing breathing support. Fall Risk Monitoring shifts the focus from physiology to patient movement and ward logistics, while Staffing and Bed Forecasting closes the loop by connecting individual risk scores to unit level resources. Together the five pages move from single organ risk to whole unit operations, and each page notes where the model is used in practice rather than only in research.
